findings.headline: KPMG has categorised Reading as Category A - audits expected to be relatively straightforward and able to sustain an ISA-compliant approach without significant difficulty.
findings.detail: Reading received the highest capacity assessment rating from MHCLG (Category A of four levels: A, B, C, D). This classification indicates the audit recovery is manageable within a defined timeline. The audit plan shows statutory reserves expected to return to unmodified opinion in 2025/26, with all other audit areas by 2026/27 or 2027/28.
findings.matters: For a lender, Category A classification is material positive news showing that the audit and financial control issues are not systemic or intractable, and the council has a clear, achievable pathway to restored audit credibility without major operational impediments.
findings.figures: Category A of four capacity levels; recovery timeline—statutory reserves 2025/26, other audit areas 2026/27-2027/28
findings.quote: We have categorised the Reading Borough Council Audit as A

findings.headline: Four years of disclaimed audit opinions covering 2021/22 through 2024/25: predecessor auditor disclaimed 2021/22-2022/23, KPMG disclaimed 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.detail: The predecessor auditor issued disclaimers for two years up to 2022/23. KPMG issued a disclaimer for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 (statutory backstop date) and for 2024/25 on 27 February 2026. This extended period of disclaimed opinions indicates unresolved audit concerns affecting the reliability of the council's financial statements.
findings.matters: Multiple years of disclaimed audit opinions signal governance or financial control weaknesses significant enough to prevent standard audit certification, a material concern for any lender assessing the council's creditworthiness and financial control environment.
findings.figures: Four years: 2021/22 and 2022/23 (predecessor auditor); 2023/24 and 2024/25 (KPMG); backstop dates 28 February 2025 and 27 February 2026
findings.quote: For Reading Borough Council this had the impact of disclaimers of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for 2 financial years up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to you previously.  For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimer of opinion on 27 February 2026.

findings.headline: New special school provision of 244 places opening September 2027 to address SEND capacity shortfall
findings.detail: Building work is progressing on two school sites to deliver new special school provision of 244 places, scheduled for opening 01/09/2027. This capital investment directly addresses the gap between 1,184 places needed for children with EHCPs and 940 currently available. However, the risk score remains at 12 despite this progress, reflecting persistent underlying financial pressure from the High Needs Block deficit.
findings.matters: Capital investment to increase in-borough SEND provision may reduce reliance on expensive out-of-borough placements, potentially moderating the pace of DSG deficit growth, though complete mitigation of the £50-97 million shortfall will require additional demand management.
findings.figures: 244 new places; opening 01/09/2027; building progressing well as of July 2026; existing shortfall 1,184 needed vs 940 available
findings.quote: As of July 2026, building work is progressing well on the identified two school sites for the key action, new special school provision.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care compliance with Care Act duties improved; waiting time reductions underway
findings.detail: The risk score for failure to meet Care Act statutory duties improved in Q2 2026-27, falling from 12 to 8 due to reduction in likelihood of breach. The paper cites operational improvement: longest overdue reviews reduced by one year. This improvement occurred despite sustained high demand of approximately 20 referrals per day, demonstrating effective performance management against a statutory safeguarding obligation.
findings.matters: Improvement in statutory compliance reduces legal and reputational liability and demonstrates effective operational management of demand under pressure, a positive indicator of financial and operational control.
findings.figures: Risk score improved 12 to 8 Q1-Q2 2026-27; longest overdue reviews reduced by one year; 20 referrals per day demand
findings.quote: Longest overdue reviews reduced by one year.

findings.headline: Cyber risk remains at highest recorded level with no improvement expected; key mitigation delayed to 2027
findings.detail: The Council's cyber risk score remains at 20 (4 impact × 5 likelihood) with expected score unchanged, placing it among the highest risks in the register. Despite 75% email interception and blocking 5,000+ monthly malicious site access attempts, the threat environment continues evolving. Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) implementation is not yet started and scheduled for 31/09/2027. Cyber Essentials Plus certification, originally targeted March 2027, is delayed due to legacy application replacement issues.
findings.matters: A sustained high-level cyber risk with no trajectory for improvement threatens the Council's operational continuity and ability to deliver services, impacting creditworthiness through both direct recovery costs and reputational damage.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 20 (unchanged); 75% of emails intercepted; 5,000+ monthly malicious link blocks; SIEM implementation scheduled 31/09/2027
findings.quote: The continuing evolution of the threat environment - not least owing to the war in Ukraine and Middle East - means that the likelihood will remain high, notwithstanding the significant set of actions in place.

findings.headline: SEND placement demand creates £97.6 million unmitigated DSG deficit by 2027-28; reduced to £50 million by 2030 with planned actions
findings.detail: The Council faces a structural deficit in the DSG High Needs Block driven by surging SEND demand. Demand modelling identified an unmitigated forecast pressure of £97.6 million by 2027-28. Planned mitigations (including opening 244 new special school places in September 2027) reduce this to £50 million by 2030. Currently, 1,972 children have EHCPs; 1,184 places are needed in specialist settings but only 940 are available.
findings.matters: A £50-97 million structural deficit in a specific budget block indicates demand-led spending growth that typically cannot be stopped; councils often carry DSG deficits forward creating cumulative financial pressure across multiple years.
findings.figures: £97.6 million unmitigated by 2027-28; £50 million mitigated by 2030; 1,972 children with EHCPs; 1,184 places needed, 940 available (244 shortfall)
findings.quote: This identified an unmitigated forecast of financial pressure, which, if not mitigated, would lead to an accrued budget pressure of £97,598,000 by 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council forecasts £5.442 million overspend for 2026-27 with no mitigation plan in place
findings.detail: The paper identifies a material budget overspend of £5.442 million forecast for 2026-27, with mitigation plans still under development. The Council has adopted a risk tolerance approach: 'no further risk mitigations will be implemented but the risk will continue to be monitored.' The overspend will require drawdown from reserves, which the Council explicitly states will jeopardise future financial stability.
findings.matters: A material unmitigated overspend requiring reserve drawdown directly threatens the council's future financial sustainability and repayment capacity, making it directly relevant to lending decisions.
findings.figures: £5.442 million overspend 2026-27; February 2026 MTFS forecast £2 million gap for 2027-28
findings.quote: There is a forecast overspend in 2026-27 of £5.442 million. Mitigation plans are being developed but are not yet in place. If the forecasted overspend is not mitigated, then this will require a further drawdown from reserves that will jeopardise the future financial stability of the Council.

findings.headline: Joint Legal Team billing process follow-up shows improvement from Limited Assurance to Reasonable Assurance, though full governance implementation remains incomplete
findings.detail: Follow-up audit of the JLT billing process found meaningful progress since the previous Limited Assurance opinion. Oversight of expenditure has improved through enhanced monitoring and senior officer review of purchase orders. Compliance with the London Boroughs' Legal Alliance procurement framework has increased. However key governance documents remain awaiting final approval, some purchase orders continue to be raised retrospectively, and work is ongoing to fully embed controls.
findings.matters: Movement from Limited to Reasonable Assurance demonstrates that financial controls over legal spending are strengthening; shows audit recommendations can drive control improvements, though full implementation remains in progress
findings.figures: Improved from Limited Assurance (prior year) to Reasonable Assurance (current); no new recommendations raised
findings.quote: meaningful progress has been made since the previous audit, which resulted in a Limited Assurance opinion. Oversight of expenditure has improved through enhanced monitoring arrangements, including regular review of purchase orders by senior officers, providing increased scrutiny and challenge over spending decisions.

findings.headline: Licensing Service audit identifies material weaknesses in Arcus system affecting data quality and operational resilience
findings.detail: The Licensing Service audit identified ongoing issues with system configuration, data quality, reporting functionality and historic data migration in the Arcus platform. These issues have reduced confidence in the completeness and reliability of licensing and financial information, increased reliance on manual compensating controls, and limited the service's ability to operate proactively. Seven recommendations were agreed with the most significant relating to the council's corporate Arcus improvement programme overseen by the CCM Programme Board.
findings.matters: System reliability directly affects operational efficiency and data quality across 5,000+ licences; manual control workarounds are less scalable and create operational risk; system remediation requires dedicated council resources
findings.figures: 7 recommendations; system supports management of over 5,000 licences
findings.quote: Ongoing issues with system configuration, data quality, reporting functionality and historic data migration have reduced confidence in the completeness and reliability of licensing and financial information. These issues increase reliance on manual controls, create operational inefficiencies and make it more difficult for the service to operate in a fully proactive and intelligence-led manner.

findings.headline: Internal Audit team capacity reduced by 0.4 FTE, with stated risk of reduced audit coverage going forward
findings.detail: The Internal Audit team experienced a reduction of 0.2 FTE from April 2026, with a further reduction of 0.2 FTE from October 2026. The committee is advised that while efforts will be made to prioritise the approved audit plan, this reduction in capacity may affect overall coverage and it may not be possible to complete all planned audits within the year.
findings.matters: Reduced audit team capacity directly reduces governance oversight across the council at a time when other audit findings suggest governance issues require sustained attention
findings.figures: 0.2 FTE reduction from April 2026; additional 0.2 FTE reduction from October 2026
findings.quote: the team experienced a small reduction in resource of 0.2 FTE from April this year, with a further reduction of 0.2 FTE from October. As a result, overall audit capacity will decrease slightly. While every effort will be made to prioritise delivery of the approved audit plan, this reduction in capacity may affect overall coverage, and it may not be possible to complete all planned audits within the year.

findings.headline: Financial Assessment & Benefits Team follow-up audit maintains Limited Assurance opinion, with assessment backlogs continuing to pressure the service
findings.detail: This follow-up audit of the FAB Team, which received Limited Assurance in 2025/26, found improvements implemented including formal triage process and Power BI dashboard. However the assurance opinion remains Limited. Audit findings identified that financial assessment backlogs continue to place pressure on the service, and further work is required to strengthen assurance over the accuracy and completeness of performance information.
findings.matters: Financial assessment is a core social care control; persistent Limited Assurance after a full year of remediation suggests underlying structural issues or implementation challenges not yet resolved
findings.figures: Audit opinion remains Limited Assurance (unchanged from 2025/26); 4 new recommendations including 2 high-priority
findings.quote: Financial assessment backlogs continue to place pressure on the service, and further work is required to strengthen assurance over the accuracy and completeness of performance information.

findings.headline: Managed payroll providers for Direct Payments received No Assurance audit opinion, with expired contracts and no documented legal protections for client funds
findings.detail: The audit found the council unable to confirm that external payroll provider arrangements comply with Contract Procedure Rules, with no procurement documentation available for review. The principal provider's contract expired in 2013 and no current contracts were identified for other providers. Significant surplus balances have accumulated with unclear ownership and accounting treatment. No formal contract management, performance monitoring or documented provider oversight arrangements were identified.
findings.matters: Client funds held by third parties are at material financial and legal risk due to governance failures; no protections documented against provider insolvency; creates reputational and compliance risk around safeguarding of vulnerable people's money
findings.figures: Principal provider contract expired 2013; 3 high-priority recommendations
findings.quote: We were unable to confirm if external payroll provider arrangements had been procured, commissioned or maintained in accordance with Contract Procedure Rules. No procurement documentation was available for review, the principal provider's contract expired in 2013, and no current contracts were identified for other providers.

findings.headline: Conflicts of interest declarations completed and embedded in routine weekly governance process
findings.detail: The council completed its first audit recommendation by introducing documented conflicts of interest declarations. Declarations are now a standing agenda item in weekly team meetings where officers confirm any relationships with council tenants or licensees. The process is minuted and monitored, with all staff having also completed annual corporate declarations.
findings.matters: Successful completion and embedding of a governance control demonstrates the council can implement audit recommendations and provides confidence it can remediate the remaining five control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Completed February 2026; declarations now weekly recurring agenda item
findings.quote: Declaration of interest reminders are included in weekly team meeting agendas and actions; team members present on 16 February 2026 confirmed nil returns

findings.headline: 70 insurance premium entries and approximately 60 older lease agreements identified as incomplete or requiring retrieval from archives
findings.detail: A cross-check of insurance records identified 70 Civica entries requiring update and discovered approximately 60 older lease agreements that need to be retrieved from archived records. The council is working with the Insurance Team to clarify responsibilities, confirm recoverable premiums, and procure reinstatement valuation work.
findings.matters: Incomplete insurance records and unretrieved lease agreements indicate gaps in control over commercial property records and suggest the council does not have full visibility of lease terms, rent review mechanisms, and insurance obligations.
findings.figures: 70 insurance entries requiring update; approximately 60 older agreements to be retrieved
findings.quote: cross-check completed on 6 May 2026 identified 70 entries requiring update; further review identified approximately 60 older agreements requiring retrieval from records.

findings.headline: 11 commercial lease debts over 12 months old identified and under recovery action
findings.detail: An aged debt report identified 11 debts over 12 months old affecting commercial lease income. These have been categorised by recovery route: referral to Legal for enforcement, payment plan negotiations with tenants, or write-off. Named cases are being actively tracked with most recent status recorded 19 May 2026.
findings.matters: Aged debts represent a collection and cashflow risk, indicating the council is not realizing expected commercial property income on schedule.
findings.figures: 11 debts over 12 months old identified
findings.quote: 11 debts over 12 months identified and categorised by action route, including Legal, officer follow-up, payment plans and write-off

findings.headline: Follow-up audit confirmed Limited Assurance opinion on commercial lease controls; full assurance cannot be given until March 2027
findings.detail: The follow-up audit confirmed a Limited Assurance opinion and identified six recommendations across rent roll income assurance, billing controls, debt management, insurance, and declarations of interest. The council states it cannot provide full assurance until reconciliation, billing control, insurance valuation and manual billing actions are completed and evidenced by 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance on a revenue stream indicates control risks that affect the council's financial sustainability, borrowing capacity and the reliability of commercial property income.
findings.figures: 6 recommendations identified; full assurance target 31 March 2027
findings.quote: The follow up audit confirmed a Limited Assurance opinion and identified a further 6 recommendations in total.

findings.paper_title: Information Governance Audit & Governance Report - 24 Sept 26
findings.headline: Cyber security is explicitly rated high-risk in the Strategic Risk Register, with ongoing threats from phishing and credential theft
findings.detail: The council faces significant and persistent cyber threats. It has implemented password audits, enhanced overseas access controls, and is developing a SASE solution. Two account compromise attempts were successfully contained during the reporting period. An external penetration test is being commissioned.
findings.matters: Cyber resilience directly affects operational continuity and data protection; high-risk rating indicates vulnerability despite active management; any successful breach could disrupt service delivery
findings.figures: 80% of inbound email traffic identified as malicious and blocked; 2 attempted account compromises successfully contained
findings.quote: The Council will therefore continue to invest in cyber security controls, staff awareness, independent security testing, and continuous monitoring to maintain an appropriate level of protection.

findings.paper_title: Information Governance Audit & Governance Report - 24 Sept 26
findings.headline: FOI response rates have degraded to 77.6% while request volume surged 29% in one year
findings.detail: Q1 2026/27 received 405 FOI requests (versus 312 in Q1 2025/26), but only 302 were answered in timescale (77.6%), compared to 310 of 312 (99.4%) the previous year. The council attributes this to volume growth and complexity of AI-generated requests, and plans council-wide training from October 2026.
findings.matters: Degrading compliance on a transparency metric while demand surges suggests resource or process constraints; persistent poor performance could damage reputation and indicate systemic capacity issues
findings.figures: 405 requests received vs 312 prior year (+29%); 77.6% in-time response rate vs 99.4% prior year
findings.quote: the Council received a total of 405 requests and 302 of these were responded to in timescales which is 77.6%. Whilst response rates have dropped, we must recognise that a total of 93 extra requests or 29% were received.

findings.paper_title: Information Governance Audit & Governance Report - 24 Sept 26
findings.headline: Subject Access Requests have surged 480% over five years (35 in 2020/21 to 203 in 2025/26), creating operational strain
findings.detail: The council faces sustained demand growth for SARs, compounded by AI-generated requests that increase complexity. The council is responding by procuring redaction software and has recruited two new Information Governance staff to address a documented backlog.
findings.matters: Growing demand for data access indicates elevated regulatory/reputational scrutiny and requires sustained operational investment; managing it poorly could signal governance weakness to external stakeholders
findings.figures: 35 requests received 2020/21, 203 requests received 2025/26; 68 cases outstanding in Q1&Q2 2026/27
findings.quote: Over the last 3 years there has been a significant increase in the volume of SARs received. At the same time, the use of AI to draft requests for SARS have added to the complexity of these cases...these factors have led to a backlog in SARs processing.

findings.headline: Council maintains strategy of deferring long-term borrowing and carries £127.234m under-borrowing managed through internal cash, noted as requiring ongoing liquidity monitoring
findings.detail: The council has taken no long-term loans during 2026/27 and continues deferring long-term borrowing while interest rates remain elevated. It manages its £127.234m under-borrowing (the gap between CFR of £676.447m and external borrowing of £523.500m) through short-term borrowing from local authorities and internal cash balances. The council explicitly notes this approach "will require ongoing monitoring in respect of the Council's cashflow requirements, long-term borrowing requirement and interest rate increases."
findings.matters: Under-borrowing through cash management depends on stable cashflow and forecast rate falls; a significant cash event or sustained high rates could force unwanted long-term borrowing.
findings.figures: External borrowing £523.500m; CFR £676.447m; under-borrowing £127.234m; Q1 short-term borrowing £146.000m at average rate 4.19%, repaid £141.000m, net increase £5.000m
findings.quote: The Council remains significantly under borrowed against its Capital Financing Requirement and is continuing to follow the approved borrowing strategy of deferring any potential long-term borrowing whilst interest rates remain at current levels and is instead utilising short or temporary borrowing from the local authority market as required.

findings.headline: Interest payable saving of £1.083m partially offsets investment shortfall, leaving net negative treasury variance of £0.200m
findings.detail: Forecast interest costs of £9.500m against budget of £10.583m create a positive variance of £1.083m. However, this saving is outweighed by the investment income shortfall, resulting in a net negative position on combined interest receivable and payable.
findings.matters: The net negative variance reduces funding below budget; while interest savings provide some benefit, the overall effect on treasury income is detrimental to the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Interest budget £10.583m, forecast £9.500m, variance £1.083m; net interest variance negative £0.200m
findings.quote: The position on interest income must be compared with external interest costs payable. The forecast external interest costs as of 30th June 2026 are £9.500m against a budget of £10.583m; a £1.083m positive variance against the General Fund budget. The net General Fund position on interest receivable/payable is therefore a net negative variance of £0.200m.

findings.headline: Investment income forecast at £1.182m against budget of £2.465m, creating an adverse variance of £1.283m
findings.detail: The council's budgeted general fund investment return for 2026/27 was £2.465m, but as of 30 June 2026 only £1.182m is forecast. Despite average investment balances of £34.064m achieving 3.82%, ahead of the SONIA benchmark of 3.73%, overall investment income significantly underperforms expectations. The budget includes interest from loans to wholly owned companies.
findings.matters: Investment income is material funding; a shortfall of this scale weakens the council's financial position and may force compensating savings or borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Budgeted £2.465m, forecast £1.182m, adverse variance £1.283m; average investment balances £34.064m earning 3.82%, SONIA benchmark 3.73%
findings.quote: The Council's budgeted General Fund investment return for 2026/27 was £2.465m; the forecast General Fund interest received from investments as of 30th June 2026 was £1.182m, a £1.283m negative variance compared to budget.

findings.headline: Housing tenancy fraud investigation recovered one property worth £78,300; multi-scheme fraud recovery generated over £150,000 in identified savings.
findings.detail: The Corporate Investigations Team reported 32 housing tenancy fraud investigations with recovery of one property (£78,300 notional savings), plus Council Tax Support savings (£1,874.95), Blue Badge enforcement (£7,146), internal investigations (£53,460), and Fraud Hub reviews (£11,814.75). Thirteen housing investigations remain ongoing.
findings.matters: The scale of housing fraud recovery and ongoing investigation pipeline indicates material fraud and overpayment risk in council services, though demonstrates council's detection and recovery capability.
findings.figures: £78,300 (housing fraud recovery); £1,874.95 + £7,146 + £53,460 + £11,814.75 across other schemes; 13 housing investigations ongoing
findings.quote: One property was recovered and 13 investigations remained ongoing. Notional savings from the recovered property totalled £78,300.

findings.headline: Financial Assessment & Benefits Team retained Limited Assurance status with assessment backlogs remaining high despite previous follow-up work.
findings.detail: Follow-up review found positive progress on seven previous recommendations but assessment backlogs remain high. Further work is required to validate performance information and provide a complete and consistent view of service performance. Four further recommendations were made, including two high-priority actions relating to performance-data verification and declarations of interest.
findings.matters: Unresolved control weaknesses in financial assessment and high backlogs could impact benefits processing accuracy, timeliness and service delivery to vulnerable adults dependent on Adult Social Care.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion retained; four further recommendations (two high-priority); seven previous recommendations partially implemented
findings.quote: assessment backlogs remain high and further work is required to validate performance information and provide a complete and consistent view of service performance. The opinion remains Limited Assurance

findings.headline: Five quarterly audits identified recurring weaknesses in data quality, performance reporting, contract oversight and manual control reliance across multiple service areas.
findings.detail: The executive summary identifies common themes across completed audits spanning multiple services, including the need to improve data quality, strengthen performance reporting, enhance contract and supplier oversight, improve documentation and audit trails, and reduce reliance on manual controls. These systemic issues appear across unrelated audit areas.
findings.matters: Systemic governance weaknesses across multiple audit areas indicate a broader internal control framework gap that could affect financial accuracy, compliance and service delivery.
findings.figures: 5 audits completed: 3 Reasonable Assurance, 1 Limited Assurance (retained), 1 No Assurance
findings.quote: several common themes emerged, including the need to improve data quality, strengthen performance reporting, enhance contract and supplier oversight, improve documentation and audit trails, and reduce reliance on manual controls.

findings.headline: Audit of Managed Payroll Providers for Direct Payments received a No Assurance opinion due to governance and procurement weaknesses.
findings.detail: The review identified significant weaknesses in governance, procurement, contractual and financial control arrangements for externally managed payroll providers handling direct payments to vulnerable adults. Assurance could not be obtained that arrangements had been procured in accordance with Contract Procedure Rules or that formal provider oversight was operating effectively. Three high-priority recommendations were made.
findings.matters: Weak controls over payroll providers managing direct payments represents a material governance and financial risk, indicating potential procurement compliance failures in a sensitive service area.
findings.figures: No Assurance opinion; three high-priority recommendations made
findings.quote: This review recorded a No Assurance opinion and identified a number of significant weaknesses within the governance, procurement, contractual and financial control arrangements relating to externally managed payroll providers.

findings.paper_title: App 1 - External Audit Progress Report Sept 26
findings.headline: Reading has an adverse budget variance of £4.6 million by Q3 2025/26 with 26% of the £11.5 million savings target assessed as non-deliverable or at risk.
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget for 2025/26 incorporating £11.5 million in planned savings. By the end of quarter 3, an adverse net variance of £4.6 million had been identified, with 26% of the savings target assessed as non-deliverable or at risk of delivery. KPMG has identified this as creating a risk of significant weakness in the council's arrangements for securing financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can balance its budget and deliver planned savings; this report shows material shortfalls in both, indicating weakness in the council's financial management arrangements.

findings.quote: The Council set a balanced budget for 2025/26, incorporating a savings target of £11.5 million. By the end of Quarter 3, an adverse net variance of £4.6 million had been identified, with 26% of the savings target assessed as non-deliverable or at risk of delivery.

findings.headline: Reading has received multiple disclaimed audit opinions in prior years
findings.detail: The paper indicates that KPMG is undertaking work to rebuild assurance following several disclaimed audit opinions. A disclaimed opinion occurs when the auditor cannot form an opinion on whether the Statement of Accounts presents a true and fair view. findings.headline: Government is considering a national Council Tax Support scheme redesign that could supersede this local scheme
findings.detail: While no immediate national changes are planned, government has indicated that Council Tax Support schemes may be reviewed soon with the possibility of reintroducing a national scheme. This would render the current redesign project obsolete and force the council to adopt new rules.
findings.matters: A national scheme change could force the council to abandon this implementation, wasting project costs and creating timing uncertainty around a major revenue collection system

findings.headline: The current scheme creates administrative and collection complexity that makes it unfit for purpose
findings.detail: Reading's current scheme, unchanged since 2022/23, requires constant recalculations and new bills due to Universal Credit's fluctuating income. This complicates debt recovery and collection. The new banded scheme aims to reduce billing churn and improve collection rates through administrative simplification.
findings.matters: Collection efficiency directly affects council cash flow and the predictability of revenue; complex billing and debt recovery processes increase arrears and reduce collection rates
findings.figures: Last year the council issued 8,500 council tax support adjustment notices against a caseload of just over 4,000 working age claimants
findings.quote: The current Council Tax Support Scheme is no longer fit for purpose, requiring regular changes to awards and the constant despatch of new bills, making it difficult for customers to understand or plan their finances as well as making administration and debt recovery complicated and expensive.

findings.headline: Interest rate environment deteriorated from forecast; expected significant cuts did not materialise
findings.detail: The council forecast significant reductions across the yield curve but received only three 0.25% Bank Rate cuts (4.50% to 3.75%). The shortfall is attributed to elevated inflation concerns, particularly from the Middle East conflict. The positive yield curve at end-March reflects inflation expectations, not growth.
findings.matters: Forecast error indicates real uncertainty about the economic path ahead. A lender needs to know whether the council is confident rates will fall further (justifying the under-borrowed position) or whether the inflation shock changes the outlook.

findings.headline: Council remains deliberately under-borrowed by £139m and took no long-term loans during the year
findings.detail: Reading is £139.028m under its Capital Financing Requirement, having taken only £245m in short-term borrowing (1 year or less) and zero long-term loans. The strategy explicitly defers long-term borrowing pending rate reductions. This positions refinancing risk: the council is using cash reserves and temporary borrowing to manage capital needs.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk concentrates into future years when temporary loans mature. The council avoided £5.172m in interest costs this year by not borrowing long-term, but this depends on rates not rising sharply. A lender needs to understand the rollover exposure if rates move against the council.

findings.paper_title: A&G Strategic Risk Register April 2026 Q4
findings.headline: Adult Social Care waiting list breach creates statutory duty risk
findings.detail: Reading has an amber-rated risk around adherence to Care Act Statutory duties because residents are waiting in Adult Social Care. The risk was downgraded from red to amber following process improvements, but indicates demand pressure and potential regulatory exposure.
findings.matters: Care Act duty breaches expose councils to regulatory action and reputational damage; waiting lists often signal either underfunding or demand surge.
findings.figures: Currently amber (reduced from red); residents described as 'waiting' with no timeline provided
findings.quote: Risk to adherence to Care Act Statutory duties as residents are waiting in Adult Social Care.

findings.paper_title: A&G Strategic Risk Register April 2026 Q4
findings.headline: Staff retention and recruitment failure is amber-rated and operational risk
findings.detail: The council identifies failure to retain and recruit staff as an amber-level risk. This reflects wider labour market pressures affecting councils and could drive service delivery degradation or cost inflation through agency spending.
findings.matters: Persistent staff turnover drives operational disruption, higher costs, and service quality issues; a material concern for service-dependent lending.
findings.figures: 1 of 6 amber risks; no specific turnover figures provided
findings.quote: Failure to retain and recruit staff.

findings.paper_title: A&G Strategic Risk Register April 2026 Q4
findings.headline: Structural SEND placement shortage driving DSG High Needs Block deficit
findings.detail: Reading has insufficient local special educational needs and disabilities provision to meet current and future demand. This red-rated risk directly impacts the Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit, a known structural funding problem.
findings.matters: DSG deficits accumulate year-on-year and force future budget reductions or require exceptional approval; they are material liabilities for a council's financial position.
findings.figures: Listed as one of 6 red risks; lack of 'local' provision implies reliance on costly independent sector placements
findings.quote: Lack of local special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) placement provision to meet current and future levels of demand and the impact on the high need's deficit.

findings.paper_title: A&G Strategic Risk Register April 2026 Q4
findings.headline: Council cannot currently deliver a balanced budget amid cost-of-living and demand pressures
findings.detail: The council is rated as having a red-level risk in its ability to deliver a balanced budget. The risk register explicitly identifies cost-of-living increases, demand pressures, and income target achievement as the drivers of this budget delivery failure risk.
findings.matters: A council unable to guarantee balanced-budget delivery is a material credit concern for lenders and signals reliance on reserves or exceptional funding.
findings.figures: 6 out of 12 total risks are red-rated; budget delivery is one of the 6 red risks
findings.quote: Unable to deliver a balanced budget because of cost-of-living increases, demand pressures and achieving income targets.

findings.headline: Gifts and Hospitality register deficiencies unresolved; inconsistency persists despite policy updates
findings.detail: A prior-year recommendation to strengthen the Gifts & Hospitality register and Declarations of Interest has not been fully resolved. While the council updated its policy and introduced new processes, the auditors' recent internal audit review shows inconsistency still remains in the register.
findings.matters: Incomplete control over conflicts of interest and declarations exposes the council to reputational, legal, and decision-quality risks; unresolved audit recommendations signal weak governance follow-through.
findings.figures: Prior-year recommendation from 2023/24; recommendation kept open as of October 2025
findings.quote: We have obtained the recent internal audit report which suggests inconsistency still remains. Hence we keep this recommendation open.

findings.headline: Gross pension liabilities of £585.1 million decreased £75.4 million but contain optimistic discount rate assumptions
findings.detail: The council's LGPS pension liability is £585.1 million, down £75.4 million year-on-year (likely due to higher discount rates). Auditors assessed overall assumptions as balanced but noted the discount rate assumption was optimistic and CPI inflation cautious, both still within reasonable ranges. A specialist is finalising work for the next committee meeting.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are long-term obligations that constrain financial flexibility; optimistic discount rate assumptions can mask the true cost of pension obligations and increase future volatility.
findings.figures: £585.1 million gross pension liabilities; £75.4 million year-on-year decrease
findings.quote: All individual assumptions were assessed as balanced and within our reasonable range except for discount rate (optimistic) and CPI inflation (cautious), but still within reasonable range.

findings.headline: General fund reserves of £49 million now being drawn down to support operations
findings.detail: The council holds £49 million in general fund reserves as of 31 March 2025. However, the 2025/26 budget assumes a £3.9 million draw and by September 2025 the council faces a £4.2 million overspend, suggesting reserves are being consumed faster than planned.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's safety net for managing deficits and shocks; rapid depletion signals the council may face liquidity constraints within 12–18 months if overspends continue.
findings.figures: £49 million general fund reserves at 31/03/2025; £3.9 million planned 2025/26 draw; £4.2 million 2025/26 overspend already reported
findings.quote: At 31/03/2025 the Council has total general fund reserves of £49million.

findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit of £24.9 million accumulated
findings.detail: The council has a £24.9 million DSG deficit, which is lower than the £26.5 million estimated in the 2024/25 MTFS. This deficit must be recovered over future years and represents a material obligation on the general fund.
findings.matters: Growing DSG deficits are a national issue but signal unsustainable education funding; councils must eventually absorb these into general budgets, further pressuring already tight finances.
findings.figures: £24.9 million DSG deficit (vs. £26.5 million forecast)
findings.quote: DSG deficit was £24.9million which is lower than the estimate of £26.5million per 2024/25 MTFS.

findings.headline: Significant weakness in governance: Council failed to identify and escalate domestic abuse prevention risks before JTAI inspection
findings.detail: A Joint Targeted Area Inspection (JTAI) identified significant weaknesses in the council's multi-agency approach to domestic abuse prevention and support for families. Auditors found that while some issues were known to the council, others were not—indicating a breakdown in risk management and escalation. This is flagged as a significant weakness in governance, not just economy/efficiency.
findings.matters: Governance failures in identifying and escalating child safeguarding risks demonstrate weak oversight and control environment, signaling broader risks across the council's operations and decision-making.
findings.figures: Joint Targeted Area Inspection issued May 2025; monitoring visit November 2025 noted progress but further work needed
findings.quote: However, we consider this as a significant weakness in governance because no evidence of the Council identifying and attempting to mitigate risks in advance of the report. Hence, we considered this is an indication of lack scrutiny and consider it as significant weakness in governance.

findings.headline: 2024/25 budget deficit of £9.3 million with only 73% of planned savings achieved
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget with £8.5 million in identified savings but achieved only 73% of those savings, resulting in a £9.3 million adverse variance. The 2025/26 budget is balanced only through a £3.9 million draw on earmarked reserves, and by September 2025 the council was already reporting a £4.2 million overspend.
findings.matters: Repeated budget misses and reliance on reserves to balance budgets signals deteriorating financial control and sustainability; drawing reserves down leaves fewer buffers for future shocks.
findings.figures: £8.5 million budgeted savings, 73% achieved; £9.3 million 2024/25 adverse variance; £3.9 million 2025/26 reserve draw assumed; £4.2 million overspend reported by September 2025
findings.quote: The Council set a balanced budget for the 2024/25 financial year with total assumed savings in the budget of £8.5 million. As at end of 2024/25, 73% of the total identified savings were achieved with an adverse net variance of £9.3 million.

findings.headline: Investment properties overvalued by £5.28 million due to optimistic yield assumptions
findings.detail: Auditors challenged the valuer's assumptions and identified that investment property valuations appeared optimistic when compared to benchmarks. The valuer revised valuations downward, but auditors still quantify an unadjusted difference of £5.28 million, meaning the council's £57.26 million investment property portfolio remains overstated in the accounts.
findings.matters: Overstated asset values inflate the council's balance sheet strength and borrowing capacity, misleading lenders about the quality and liquidity of the council's asset base.
findings.figures: £57.26 million investment property portfolio; £5.28 million unadjusted valuation difference; originally overstated by £10.23 million before valuer's revision
findings.quote: We identified a number of judgements regarding asset yields within our sampled population that appear optimistic when compared to comparable asset benchmarks. We have challenged the valuer with KPMG's suite of benchmarks and property sale evidence, who updated their valuation as a result.

findings.headline: Auditors issuing disclaimer opinion due to insufficient assurance over prior-year reserves and comparatives
findings.detail: KPMG will issue a disclaimer opinion on the financial statements because they lack assurance over the split of usable and unusable reserves and comparative figures for 2023/24. This stems from prior years not receiving full audits under the statutory backstop. The auditors plan to perform substantive testing in FY2026 to reduce this to a qualified opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion signals the auditors cannot verify core financial position statements—critical information for lenders assessing the council's financial health and reserve strength.
findings.figures: Opening reserves split unverified; comparative figures for 2023/24 balance sheet and income/expenditure cannot be assured
findings.quote: Given our work to rebuild assurance is not complete we do not have assurance over the split of useable and unusable reserves and we have determined that there is insufficient time to complete our audit to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the financial statements as a whole.

findings.headline: Planned capital programme requires £153.97m new borrowing over three years, with projected CFR increase of £100.45m
findings.detail: The 2026/27-2028/29 Capital Programme totals £323.237m (£118.607m General Fund, £204.630m HRA). After grants, s106 contributions and capital receipts, the council needs to borrow £153.970m. After accounting for Minimum Revenue Provision charges of £53.524m, the Capital Financing Requirement is projected to increase by £100.446m across the period.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know the scale of new borrowing and how it will be serviced. The council is signalling material capital investment but also relying on temporary borrowing markets to finance it, which depends on continued access and favourable rates.
findings.figures: Capital programme £323.237m; new borrowing requirement £153.970m; projected CFR increase £100.446m
findings.quote: The Capital Programme 2026/27-2028/29 totals £323.237m (£118.607m General Fund and £204.630m HRA)... the total borrowing requirement is £153.970m... the Council has a projected increase in its CFR of £100.446m

findings.headline: Council carrying £170m temporary borrowing portfolio, betting on interest rate cuts to defer long-term borrowing
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, the council has £170m in temporary borrowing outstanding, including two £50m PWLB HRA loans with one-year terms maturing in 2026/27. Rather than lock in long-term debt, the council plans to continue using cheaper temporary borrowing, deliberately deferring long-term borrowing to avoid 'cost of carry' if rates fall. This strategy depends entirely on interest rate forecasts proving correct.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's debt strategy depends on optimistic rate forecasts. The council has £100m of temporary borrowing maturing within the planning period; if rates do not fall as assumed or if they rise, the council faces refinancing risk and potential carry costs on deferred long-term borrowing.
findings.figures: £170.000m temporary borrowing outstanding; £100.000m maturing within one year (two £50.000m loans)
findings.quote: As at 31st December 2025, the Council had an outstanding temporary borrowing portfolio of £170.000m... This includes two £50.000m loans taken from the PWLB utilising the HRA certainty rate, both of which have one year terms.

findings.headline: Council repaid £5m LOBO loan in response to lender's proposed rate increase
findings.detail: The council recently exercised its option to repay a £5m Lender Option Borrower Option loan when the lender proposed changing the interest rate. LOBO loans give the lender unilateral rights to change terms, so the council's decision to repay signals both awareness of rate risk and active management of debt exposure.
findings.matters: Lenders want to see councils managing exposure to rate-rise risk. The willingness and ability to prepay when terms are pushed is a strength, but the incident also signals that the council is encountering rate pressures in the market.
findings.quote: The Council has recently taken their option to repay the outstanding £5.000m LOBO following the lenders proposed change in interest rate.

findings.headline: Reading Transport Limited experiencing difficult financial year due to fare revenue collapse
findings.detail: The wholly-owned bus operator is facing declining fare-paying passengers and increasing costs. Expected to return to profitability in 2026/27, but the turnaround is not assured and may require subsidy or asset write-downs.
findings.matters: Losses in wholly-owned companies can quickly become unexpected calls on the general fund if trading does not recover as forecast.
findings.figures: Not specified; described as 'difficult year financially'
findings.quote: Reading Transport Limited (RTL) – The company is experiencing a difficult year financially due to a decline in fare-paying passengers and increasing costs but is expected to return to profitability in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account requires £3.108m to £3.708m annual reserve drawdowns across three years
findings.detail: The HRA 30-year business plan will draw between £2.849m and £3.708m from reserves annually in 2026/27 to 2028/29 to balance. This limits reserves available for unforeseen housing stock issues.
findings.matters: HRA reserve depletion reduces the council's ability to respond to emergency repairs, stock condition deterioration, or housing demand spikes without borrowing.
findings.quote: A balanced budget is delivered across all three years with a drawdown from reserves of £3.108m in 2026/27, £2.849m in 2027/28 and £3.708m in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Reading excluded from £865m government recovery grant allocation, receiving baseline funding only
findings.detail: Outside Fair Funding 2.0, £865m is allocated via Recovery Grant and related schemes to other councils. Reading receives none of this. Over three years, Reading receives only £6.264m in additional core spending power funding (£3.562m in 2026/27, declining thereafter).
findings.matters: Exclusion from exceptional grants suggests the government does not view Reading as having exceptional need, despite documented SEND crisis and unbalanced future years; limits future bailout options.
findings.figures: Reading receives £0 of £865m recovery grant allocation; £6.264m over 3 years in core spending power vs £4.277m in 2025/26
findings.quote: Reading Borough Council will receive none of this £865 million.

findings.headline: Adult social care demand pressures require £4.700m additional investment in 2026/27
findings.detail: Increases in service users, complexity of care packages, demographic shifts to younger service users, and contract inflation are driving a £4.700m net increase. Combined with children's growth, social care investment exceeds £8.5m in one year.
findings.matters: Social care is the largest demand pressure facing councils nationally; Reading's figures are consistent with sector crisis but place it in a financially constrained position.
findings.figures: £4.700m net increase for Adult Social Care in 2026/27
findings.quote: This updated MTFS includes a net increase of £4.700m for Adult Social Care services in 2026/27 to address these pressures, in addition to the capital investment in facilities.

findings.headline: Children's social care spending growth of £3.843m flagged as 'unsustainable'
findings.detail: The budget includes £3.843m additional investment in children's placements and new residential homes in 2026/27 alone. The council explicitly states this upward trend is unsustainable, acknowledging the problem without a solution.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in social care are the leading cause of council financial failure; an unsustainable trajectory indicates a structural mismatch between need and funding.
findings.figures: £3.843m net increase in 2026/27; described as unsustainable trend
findings.quote: this updated MTFS invests significant additional funds in Children's Social Care placements, with a net increase of £3.843m budgeted in 2026/27, and in the provision of new residential homes, but the upward trend is unsustainable.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced through £7.302m one-off draw from earmarked reserves, including £2.797m from smoothing reserve
findings.detail: The budget relies on drawdowns from specific reserves (£4.169m), the Collection Fund Smoothing Reserve (£2.797m), and the Financial Resilience Reserve (£0.336m). The smoothing reserve draw is one-off, and if the collection fund position deteriorates, the council loses a key buffer.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite and one-off sources; recurring use signals underlying imbalance. Loss of smoothing reserve flexibility reduces the council's ability to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: £7.302m total drawdown; £2.797m from Collection Fund Smoothing Reserve; £0.336m from Financial Resilience Reserve
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Budget is balanced by an overall £7.302m assumed draw on (contribution from) earmarked reserves, consisting of: £2.797m from the Collection Fund Smoothing Reserve to fund the one-off deficit in 2026/27; £0.336m from the Financial Resilience Reserve to balance the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: £3.878m of planned savings (26% of MTFS target) currently at risk of non-delivery
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes £14.781m of savings over three years, but the 2025/26 Q2 monitoring report flagged £3.878m at risk. Of this, £0.998m is likely to carry forward into 2026/27. This raises questions about delivery capability against an already tight plan.
findings.matters: If savings targets fail, the council has little flexibility given the reserve drawdowns and unbalanced future years; delivery risk is high.
findings.figures: £14.781m assumed savings over 3 years; £3.878m at risk; £0.998m likely to slip into 2026/27
findings.quote: £3.878m of savings are currently at risk of non-delivery, with £0.998m likely to be carried forward into 2026/27 following a review undertaken as part of the 2026/27 budget setting process

findings.headline: Budget unbalanced in 2027/28 (£1.996m gap) and 2028/29 (£0.207m gap) with no identified solution
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget is balanced through £7.302m in reserve drawdowns, but the indicative budgets for 2027/28 and 2028/29 show unresolved gaps. The council acknowledges future savings must be found but does not specify how or where.
findings.matters: Unbalanced future-year budgets indicate the current approach is not sustainable and places the council in an ongoing cycle of late-year budget repairs.
findings.quote: The indicative budgets for 2027/28 and 2028/29 are not currently balanced with a budget gap of £1.996m currently forecast for 2027/28, reducing to a gap of £0.207m for 2028/29.

findings.headline: SEND deficit of £48.627m would have triggered section 114 notice without government bailout
findings.detail: The high needs block deficit reached £48.627m by March 2026 and was forecast to reach £94.303m by March 2028 when the statutory override ends. The council's own reserves are insufficient to cover this. However, the February 2026 settlement announced 90% government funding, reducing the deficit to £4.863m, but the council must fund the remaining 10% and any further deficits through 2027/28.
findings.matters: A s114 notice is a formal declaration of financial inability to meet expenditure and stops most council spending; this was a systemic risk that only government intervention averted.
findings.figures: £48.627m cumulative deficit by 31 March 2026; forecast to £94.303m by March 2028; government funds 90% leaving £4.863m for council; council reserves insufficient to fund the full amount
findings.quote: Council reserves will not be sufficient to fund this deficit, potentially triggering the need to issue a s114 notice. It is therefore critical that action is taken to address the deficit.

findings.headline: Staffing recruitment failures driving income shortfalls: Building Control, Planning, and Fleet unable to fill posts, each creating 6-figure pressures
findings.detail: Building Control has failed recent recruitment rounds and cannot fill qualified surveyor posts, resulting in lost fee income of £0.151m plus inability to reduce expensive agency staffing (net £0.047m adverse). Planning staffing pressures total £0.082m. Fleet hire costs spike £0.415m due to vehicle unreliability when permanent recruitment delays continue.
findings.matters: Persistent recruitment failure in professional services signals either uncompetitive pay/conditions or deeper labour market issues. Each unfilled post represents lost income or higher contractor costs. This pattern across multiple services suggests systemic HR or budget constraints.
findings.figures: Building Control: £0.151m income loss, £0.047m net staffing adverse variance; Planning: £0.082m staffing/running expenses pressure; Fleet: £0.415m adverse variance including hire cost escalation
findings.quote: There is an adverse variance on income generation of £0.151m. This income shortfall directly correlates to the lack of qualified staff to undertake the fee earning work. Recent rounds of recruitment have been unsuccessful in appointing permanent staff and there is a positive variance for permanent staff costs, however hopes of reducing use of agency staff and their costs have not been realised.

findings.headline: Significant capital programme slippage: £9.911m reprogrammed out of 2025/26 General Fund, £16.422m out of HRA Capital
findings.detail: Of the £86.5m General Fund capital budget, £9.911m is being reprogrammed to future years (11% slippage), including £4.67m of grant-funded education schemes and £2m for Minster Quarter brownfield scheme. HRA Capital shows even larger slippage of £16.422m (20% of £80.933m budget), dominated by £19.138m New Build & Acquisitions phase 2-4 scheme delays.
findings.matters: Large capital reprogramming indicates delivery risk. Schools funding is grant-dependent; if education builds slip, grants may be recycled. New build delay suggests housing supply targets at risk. For a council under financial pressure, undelivered capital projects also mean forgone cost savings or income streams.
findings.figures: General Fund: £9.911m reprogrammed out (11% of £86.5m); HRA: £16.422m reprogrammed (20% of £80.933m); largest items £4.67m education, £2m Minster Quarter, £19.138m New Build phase 2-4
findings.quote: A net total of £9.911m of budgets are requested to be reprogrammed between 2025/26 and future years of the Capital Programme... This includes: £4.670m for grant funded Education schemes, to correctly reflect the timescales of the programme of works; £2.000m for the Minster Quarter - Brownfield Land Grant Element scheme, to reflect current expectations of timings for this scheme

findings.headline: £6.738m overdue sundry debt with £2.428m aged over 2 years; debt concentration in Adult Social Care
findings.detail: General Fund has £6.738m overdue sundry debt. Of this, £2.428m is over 2 years old (34% of overdue balance). 77.5% of this aged debt is concentrated in Adult Social Care, suggesting deep collection issues in social care charging or placement cost recovery.
findings.matters: Old, concentrated debt suggests systemic collection failure in a specific area. Social care debt may reflect disputes over charging, cost-of-living pressures on service users, or weak enforcement. It will not be recovered.
findings.figures: £6.738m total overdue; £2.428m over 2 years old (34% of total); 77.5% of aged debt in Adult Social Care
findings.quote: Total General Fund overdue sundry debt as at the end of Quarter 2 is £6.738m... Split of General Fund Debt by Directorate... 77.5% Community & Adult Social Care

findings.headline: Council Tax collection declining: 0.93% below prior year, worth £1.423m
findings.detail: Council Tax collection rates are behind both 2024/25 and pre-pandemic 2019/20 levels, attributed to ongoing cost-of-living crisis. A 0.93% underperformance is worth approximately £1.423m to the Collection Fund in 2025/26. The council also discontinued discretionary Local Council Tax Support on 31 March 2025, which may further pressure future collections.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the largest guaranteed revenue stream. Collection decline signals both residents in financial stress (a demand indicator) and less certain cash flow for the council.
findings.figures: 0.93% collection rate decline vs 2024/25; worth ~£1.423m to Collection Fund 2025/26; 2.11% below 2019/20 pre-pandemic level
findings.quote: Council Tax collection rates are behind the collection levels at the same point when compared to pre-Covid-19 pandemic rates (2019/20) and 2024/25 collection rates at the same point last year... a 0.93% decrease in collection is worth approximately £1.423m to the Collection Fund for 2025/26.

findings.headline: Council drawing down reserves faster than planned: HRA reserves £0.197m more than budgeted, with General Fund using £1.844m additional releases
findings.detail: HRA now forecasts a £5.244m drawdown from reserves instead of the budgeted £5.047m, a £0.197m deterioration driven by repair and maintenance pressures. The General Fund is using £1.844m more in earmarked reserves than planned, primarily to mitigate Children's Services pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves are a one-off buffer; they deplete. Drawing them down faster signals the council is running structural deficits it cannot fund from ongoing operations. Once depleted, the council faces either service cuts or borrowing.
findings.figures: HRA forecast drawdown £5.244m vs budgeted £5.047m (£0.197m adverse); General Fund additional reserve release £1.844m
findings.quote: At Quarter 2, the forecast revenue outturn position on the HRA is an adverse net variance to budget of £0.197m... Therefore, a drawdown from the HRA Reserve is forecast of £5.244m rather than the approved budgeted £5.047m drawdown from reserves.

findings.headline: Only 66% of planned savings are either delivered or on track; £3.878m (34%) either non-deliverable or at risk
findings.detail: Of £11.516m total savings required, £3.975m (34%) delivered to date and £3.663m (32%) on track. However, £2.143m (19%) are categorised as non-deliverable (red) and £1.735m (15%) at risk of delivery (amber). This leaves the council exposed to unmitigated pressures in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver its own savings plan loses credibility on financial management and signals either weak project discipline or unrealistic budget-setting. Any slippage in the red/amber figures directly worsens the outturn.
findings.figures: £2.143m (19%) non-deliverable; £1.735m (15%) at risk; only £3.975m of £11.516m (34%) delivered to date

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand surging: 189 new service users in 6 months, with escalating referral trends in support categories

This variance comprises a £0.123m income pressure which is directly related to the number of planning applications, which includes £0.055m of red rated savings (Appendix 2). These have been impacted by successive development risks such as inflation, materials costs, changes in legislation and market factors such as high costs of mortgages.

findings.headline: Council tax collection falling 0.48% behind prior year following end of discretionary support
findings.detail: Q1 collection rate is 27.0%, down from 27.5% in 2024/25 and 28.1% pre-pandemic (2019/20). The decline is attributed to the cost of living crisis. Crucially, discretionary support eligibility for Local Council Tax Support recipients ended on 31 March 2025, which the report expects will impact collection further.
findings.matters: Declining collection reduces the certainty of the revenue base. The removal of discretionary welfare support suggests collection pressure will persist or worsen in 2025/26.
findings.quote: Council Tax collection rates are behind the collection levels at the same point when compared to pre-Covid-19 pandemic rates (2019/20) and 2024/25 collection rates at the same point last year. This is a similar trend across Berkshire and is likely related to the continuing cost of living crisis. It should be noted that the Council's discretionary support to eligible customers in receipt of Local Council Tax Support, which had been in place in recent financial years, ceased on 31st March 2025 which may impact on collection rates from 2025/26.

findings.headline: Adult social care demand continues to grow despite containment plans
findings.detail: Service users increased from 1,755 on 1 April 2025 to 1,796 by 30 June—a net growth of 41 in Q1. The report flags risk of further growth of £3m if 2024/25 trajectory repeats (115 net service users at £3.6m cost).
findings.matters: Despite a recovery plan that balances the current-year budget, the underlying demand trend is unfavourable and could require further contingency spending in future years.
findings.figures: Service users 1,755 to 1,796 (+41 in Q1). Risk: further growth of 115 service users at ~£3m cost.
findings.quote: The service users in place on 1st April 2025 was an average of 1,755 and by 30th June 2025 these had increased to 1,796. In addition to the current forecast, there is a risk that demand increases over the remainder of the year in line with the increase in 2024/25, which was 115 service users at a cost of approximately £3.600m.

findings.headline: Savings delivery slippage of £1.9m, leaving one-third of £11.5m target at risk or undelivered
findings.detail: Of £11.516m total 2025/26 savings target, £1.888m (16%) is categorised as non-deliverable (red) and £2.024m (18%) is at risk (amber). Only 66% are either delivered or on track. The report notes that £1.837m of prior-year savings were not delivered and have been carried forward.
findings.matters: Persistent year-on-year savings slippage is a material control risk. If the council cannot reliably deliver savings plans, the budget position becomes dependent on reserves or further cuts during the year.

findings.headline: Children's social care costs accelerating beyond budget despite stable caseload
findings.detail: Brighter Futures for Children is forecasting a £5.21m adverse variance. Between January and July 2025, placement costs rose by £5.5m: 10 new placements added at over £100k each (£2.264m), and 12 existing placements saw cost increases over £100k each (£3.587m). This reflects care package escalations and placement breakdowns, not new children entering the system.
findings.matters: The cost per child is rising materially even as the total number of children looked after remains stable, suggesting structural cost drivers that won't be resolved by demand management alone. This is a structural budget risk.
findings.figures: Budget was £10.212m (2023/24), £17.134m (2024/25), £22.473m (2025/26). Forecast variance £5.210m. Net increase £5.5m Jan-July 2025.
findings.quote: A detailed review of placement changes between the January 2025 forecast and the actual position in July 2025 has identified a net increase of £5.5m, including: • 10 new placements were added for children coming into care, with an individual forecast cost exceeding £0.100m, totalling £2.264m. • 12 existing placements saw an increase in forecast cost of more than £0.100m, totalling £3.587m.

news_drafts.headline: Reading faces £5.334m spending pressure but key savings lack contingency plans
news_drafts.lead: Reading Council has reported a spending pressure of £5.334m for the first quarter. Children's Services accounts for £4.020m of this, driven by rising demand, increasing placement costs for children in care and residential provision, and continued reliance on agency workers. The council is depending on a £6.285m savings programme to close the gap. However, the scheme carries substantial delivery risk. The council's single largest saving—a £2.6m reduction to the Adult Social Care placement budget—remains in mid-stages of delivery with no contingency funding set aside despite being its most material item. Additionally, vacancy factor savings worth £489k across three services lack any identified funding source.

news_drafts.headline: Reading Council forecasts £5.3m budget pressure at quarter one, driven by children's services costs
news_drafts.lead: Reading Council is forecasting a net pressure of £5.334m across its General Fund budget at the first quarter of the financial year, with Children's Services alone accounting for £4.020m of the shortfall. The pressure is being driven by rising placement costs — the fees paid to residential and foster care providers — combined with increasing demand for statutory services and continued reliance on agency workers, the council's monitoring report shows. Only 15% of planned savings in Children's Services have completed their delivery milestones so far. Economic Growth and Neighbourhood Services is forecasting a further £0.925m pressure, while Council Tax and business rates collection have both fallen behind last year's levels, with the council attributing the decline to the cost of living crisis. The council is attempting mitigations focused on placement stability and fee negotiation, but the underlying pressure reflects demand that the budget was not built to accommodate.

news_drafts.headline: Reading reports £5.3m spending pressure at quarter one, driven mainly by children's services placement costs and low savings delivery
news_drafts.lead: Reading Council is forecasting a net spending pressure of £5.334m in the General Fund at the end of the first quarter, with nearly three-quarters of the shortfall in Children's Services. The service is facing £4.020m of pressure, driven by rising placement costs, increased demand for statutory services and reliance on agency workers. At quarter one, only 15 per cent of Children's Services' planned savings had reached completion milestones; 43 per cent remain in mid-stages of delivery. The council has set a savings target of £6.285m for the year but is forecasting only £0.578m of this as a pressure across the General Fund, suggesting substantial savings plans have not yet been built into forecast costs. The council's Policy Committee received the quarterly performance report on 16 September.
